nature-nbs-119.title: International standards for doing restoration well
nature-nbs-119.text: Restoration needs a rulebook as much as a shovel. The Society for Ecological Restoration publishes international standards that set out principles for planning, doing and monitoring restoration projects. The first edition came out on December 12, 2016, and the second on September 27, 2019. They recommend performance measures for industries, communities and governments. A technical appendix covers how to source seeds for restoration.

nature-nbs-116.title: Restoration ecology and conservation biology: sister sciences
nature-nbs-116.text: Two sciences share a love of habitat but look at it differently. Conservation biology studies species populations and often centers on animals. Restoration ecology works at the level of whole communities and centers on plants, because projects usually start by establishing plant communities. It also puts more weight on soils, fungi and microbes, the base of land ecosystems. Both value protecting and restoring habitat. Restoration ecology became a separate field in the late twentieth century.

nature-nbs-118.title: The gap between restoration science and practice
nature-nbs-118.text: Researchers and the people who restore land often talk past each other. A 2009 survey ranked this divide as the second most cited limit on the growth of restoration science and practice. Land managers often find research questions not useful. Studies tend to be small and controlled, unlike real projects. Tight budgets mean many projects keep few records, which limits evidence-based advice.

nature-nbs-120.title: Traditional ecological knowledge: restoration's long history
nature-nbs-120.text: Restoration is not a modern invention. Indigenous peoples have built up knowledge by observing and managing their environment, and it shows restoration practiced for thousands of years. They shaped vegetation to meet their needs and sometimes increased populations and biodiversity. California Indians, for example, used concentrated forest burning. Because such knowledge is tied to place, restorers must take care not to appropriate it. Projects involving Indigenous peoples should be led by them.

nature-nbs-148.title: Mine reclamation: turning a pit back into land
nature-nbs-148.text: Many abandoned mines were never reclaimed at all. Mine reclamation is reshaping mined land so it again works as an ecosystem or can be used economically. It happens after mining ends, but it may be planned before a mine is even permitted. The practice began at the start of the 20th century. Full return to the original landscape is often impossible. Usually the realistic limit is making mine waste physically and chemically stable. In open-cut mines, rock backfills the pit, stored soil and topsoil go on top, and vegetation is restored. Reforestation is the main way of restoring these sites. The money side is built into law in the United States. Under the 1977 SMCRA law, operators post a performance bond equal to the cost of their reclamation plan. They get it back only after reclamation succeeds. A coal tax of $0.12 per ton mined underground and $0.28 per ton surface-mined pays to reclaim abandoned mines.

nature-nbs-132.title: Active rewilding: giving nature a hand
nature-nbs-132.text: Not all rewilding means walking away. Active rewilding covers approaches that involve human intervention. It can mean reintroducing or moving species, engineering habitat, and removing man-made structures and troublesome introduced species. Across the field, methods range from protecting land and linking habitats to removing infrastructure and bringing species back.

nature-nbs-136.title: The case against rewilding
nature-nbs-136.text: Rewilding has opponents among governments, farmers and conservationists. Some officials say strict no-extraction areas limit people's ability to earn a living; others reply that ecotourism creates jobs. Some farmers say it abandons productive farmland while world population grows. Some scientists say its benefits lack evidence and that it may pull funding from better-supported conservation. Reintroduced predators can also cause conflict, as brown bears have in Trentino, Italy. Supporters and critics still disagree on its economic and conservation effects.

nature-nbs-135.title: Ecosystem engineers: the animals rewilding relies on
nature-nbs-135.text: A beaver dam can remake a valley. Ecosystem engineers are living things that clearly reshape the structure of their habitats, and large mammals are prime examples. Rewilding uses beaver, elephants, bison and elk. Where the originals are extinct, cattle and pigs stand in for aurochs and wild boar.

nature-nbs-133.title: Pleistocene rewilding: bringing back Ice Age giants
nature-nbs-133.text: Many of today's ecosystems evolved alongside huge animals that are now gone. Pleistocene rewilding is bringing back surviving Ice Age megafauna, or close stand-ins for extinct ones, to restore how ecosystems work. Advocates say ecosystems that lost their large mammals may collapse. Critics answer that today's communities cannot be assumed to work like those of 10,000 years ago. The two sides still disagree on whether this can work.

nature-nbs-134.title: Trophic rewilding: putting predators back at the top
nature-nbs-134.text: At Oostvaardersplassen in the Netherlands, grazing animals multiplied and then starved in large numbers. Trophic rewilding aims to prevent that. It restores food-web interactions, especially top predators controlling plant-eaters, by bringing species back so ecosystems regulate themselves. Apex predators may be needed to stop grazers over-breeding and stripping vegetation. How predators do this is debated: mainly by killing prey, or indirectly through fear.

nature-nbs-141.title: The Trillion Tree Campaign
nature-nbs-141.text: Earth holds about 3 trillion trees, Tom Crowther found in 2015. The Trillion Tree Campaign aims to plant one trillion more to fight climate change. Planting 1.2 trillion was later estimated to offset 10 years of human CO2 emissions. It grew out of the Billion Tree Campaign, inspired by Wangari Maathai and launched by UNEP in 2006. In December 2011 UNEP handed it to the youth-led Plant-for-the-Planet Foundation. By 30 May 2021, 13.96 billion trees had been planted, 1.396% of the goal.

nature-nbs-123.title: Who pays for restoring forest landscapes
nature-nbs-123.text: Restoring a landscape takes money long before it pays back. Financing comes in two broad kinds: for-profit, such as debt or loans, and not-for-profit, such as grants, fiscal policy or public spending. FAO says linking smallholders with investors, local ownership and blended finance help restoration reach scale. Barriers remain: a lack of large-scale government funding, and smallholders' limited resources and skills.

nature-nbs-125.title: Bringing forests back after fire
nature-nbs-125.text: Fire is a heavy cause of forest loss in many parts of the world. Some fires are set to clear land for crops; others occur naturally or on purpose in dry areas. Burnt land can lose much of its ecosystem value and degrade further through erosion and desertification. Restoring it is not always the answer, though. Sometimes fire raises a site's biodiversity, and plans then look for a different land use.

nature-nbs-124.title: Fencing out deer to save young forests
nature-nbs-124.text: Deer and other browsing animals can eat a young forest before it grows up. Over-grazed saplings may be damaged beyond recovery, which reduces biodiversity. Restorers shield regrowth with deer fencing. Where fencing is too costly, they plant trees that can recover their structure after browsing.

nature-nbs-157.title: Does restoring nature pay for itself?
nature-nbs-157.text: On average, the benefits of ecosystem restoration exceed the initial investment tenfold. Doing nothing costs at least three times as much as restoring. This comparison of costs, benefits and inaction is what cost-effectiveness means here. The sums are large. Degradation of land and marine ecosystems costs about 10% of annual global GDP, around $6.3 trillion. Restoring 350 million hectares by 2030 could generate US$9 trillion in ecosystem services and remove 13 to 26 gigatons of greenhouse gases. UK peatland restoration by 2027 was estimated to yield £191 million a year after costs. In Oregon, each dollar invested generated another 1.4 to 2.4 dollars of economic activity. Cheaper methods help, such as {{ref:nature-nbs-138}}, which skips site preparation and raising seedlings. One warning: when clean-up costs fall late in a project, a high discount rate makes it look better than it is.

nature-nbs-101.title: The restoration economy: jobs from repairing nature
nature-nbs-101.text: In Oregon, every million invested in restoration created 15-24 jobs. That is the restoration economy at work: economic activity that comes from repairing land and nature. It is set against activity built on sprawl or on using up natural resources. The idea is that repairing past damage often pays off at local, regional and national scales. The phrase spread after Storm Cunningham's 2002 book The Restoration Economy, which sorted restorative development into eight sectors. Four focus on nature: ecological, watershed and fishery restoration, plus {{ref:nature-nbs-258}}. Projects need workers, materials and services, so spending creates local jobs and business. The Oregon study found each dollar generated another 1.4 to 2.4 dollars, with effects similar to road building. The jobs have a downside. Hand work such as tree planting pays less than logging, is less reliable, and is mostly done by immigrant workers.

nature-nbs-152.title: Anthromes: the biomes people have remade
nature-nbs-152.text: Most land is no longer wild in the old sense. Anthromes are the land's biomes in their modern, human-altered form, mapped by patterns of lasting human land use. Each is a patchwork of uses, often with areas partly reclaimed by nature. Groups include croplands, pastures, plantations and cities, and artificial wetlands such as reservoirs and rice paddies.

nature-nbs-151.title: Three ways to handle a novel ecosystem
nature-nbs-151.text: Managers facing a novel ecosystem have three choices: tolerate it, manage against it toward history, or manage for it as a new system. Too little funding and information have made tolerance the default. Managing against it is traditional restoration, removing non-native species and bringing back natives. But fast climate change often makes historical baselines unreachable, so scientists increasingly aim for resilient, adaptive ecosystems. Managing for novelty remains the more controversial path.

nature-nbs-147.title: Restoring land lost to the desert
nature-nbs-147.text: Moving sand dunes must be stopped before anything else can grow. Restoring desertified land happens in phases. First, grasses, shelterbelts and woodlots fix the soil. Shelterbelts are rows of trees set across the prevailing wind. Next, nitrogen-fixing plants enrich the soil and crops are grown at once. The crops are rotated yearly so they do not drain trace elements.

nature-nbs-144.title: Mine rehabilitation bonds: paying for repair up front
nature-nbs-144.text: Before mining starts, a company can be made to put money down. A rehabilitation security bond is that money, a guarantee that the company will repair the land afterward. Australian bonds total $9.49 billion, with New South Wales holding $2.68bn in 2019. Its Auditor General questioned whether they cover full costs. Enforced, such rules could create regional jobs. Reclaiming abandoned US mines is estimated to cost $9.6bn.

nature-nbs-142.title: Exclosures: fencing animals out so land can regreen
nature-nbs-142.text: A fence can heal a hillside. An exclosure is a fenced-off patch of grazing land that keeps out cattle, deer or other browsing animals. Most are set aside for regreening, with no wood cutting or grazing. People still earn from them through grass harvesting, beekeeping and other products. In Tigray, Ethiopia, carbon credits for stored CO2 fund village priorities.

nature-nbs-149.title: The Forestry Reclamation Approach for coal land
nature-nbs-149.text: Old coal mines can grow forests again if the ground is right. The Forestry Reclamation Approach is a set of guidelines for regrowing forest on land mined for coal. It calls for at least four feet of good rooting material, such as topsoil or weathered sandstone, loosely graded to avoid compaction. Early successional trees go in first for wildlife and soil, then valuable crop trees.

nature-nbs-140.title: AFR100: Africa's pledge to restore 100 million hectares
nature-nbs-140.text: Africa has its own regional share of the {{ref:nature-nbs-139}}. AFR100, the African Forest Landscape Restoration Initiative, aims to bring 100 million hectares of degraded land under restoration by 2030. So far 28 African countries have committed a total of 113 million hectares. Latin America's Initiative 20x20 is a similar effort, aiming to restore 20 million hectares by 2030.

nature-nbs-128.title: Rewetting peatlands to stop them leaking carbon
nature-nbs-128.text: Drained peat rots, and rotting releases greenhouse gases. Rewetting returns a drained peatland to its waterlogged state so peat-forming plants recover. Workers block and fill drainage canals and dam gullies with peat or plastic. A higher water table slows decay and cuts emissions. Wet peat makes some methane, but methane stays in the air for a shorter time, so the long-run effect is likely cooling.

nature-nbs-130.title: What restored peatlands are worth
nature-nbs-130.text: Restoring 20% of Scotland's peatland was estimated to bring benefits of £80 to £336 million a year. Such estimates compare the money value society gains from restoring peatlands with what restoration costs. A later study found UK restoration by 2027 would yield £191 million a year after costs. Delaying until 2039–2050 would lose much of that benefit.

nature-nbs-296.title: Paludiculture: farming on wet peat
nature-nbs-296.text: Peatlands cover only 3% of land but store more than 450 gigatonnes of carbon, more than all forests. Paludiculture is farming on drained peatlands after they have been rewetted. Raising the water table gets the carbon store working again, so the land serves as both carbon sink and farm. Crops include berries, herbs, timber and biomass for biofuel. Whether a given practice counts as sustainable paludiculture is debated.

reviews.restoring-land-and-forests: Repairing nature takes many forms, from replanting lost forests and helping seedlings regrow to stepping back and letting wild processes return. The money can add up: restoration benefits are estimated to exceed the investment tenfold, and repair work creates local jobs. Yet up to 90% of planted seedlings often fail, plantations of one or two species lack the wildlife of natural forest, and pledges like the {{ref:nature-nbs-139}} often hide land set aside for wood. Carbon stored in new forests can return to the air through fire or harvest. Above all, restoration is too slow to make up for delays in cutting fossil fuel emissions.
